mstts:express-as.prosody: Welcome—I'm so glad you're here with me for this journey. Imagine, for a moment, living in London, where each sunrise brings the echo of distant bombs and every nightfall feels uncertain. Life goes on, but everything is changed—ordinary routines take on new meaning, and every day is colored by a mix of fear and surprising strength. That’s exactly the world we step into together through the pages of World War II London Blitz Diary, Volume 1, brought to life by Ruby Side Thompson. Her diary draws us right into the heart of wartime London. We get to witness the city’s pulse—neighbors leaning on each other, families holding onto hope, and individuals wrestling with their worries, yet still finding those small moments of joy. What’s truly special is how these entries let us feel both the devastation overhead and the quiet, everyday courage inside. It’s not just about the bombs or the blackout nights; it’s about sharing laughter in shelters and savoring the little victories, even as the city transforms around them. As we explore these stories, we’re invited to reflect on how adversity shapes not just one person, but entire communities—and how the human spirit can shine, even in the darkest of times. So, let’s step into this extraordinary diary together, and discover what it truly means to survive, remember, and hope.

Chapter One: The Calm Before the Storm—Ordinary Life on the Edge of War.
Imagine London, just before everything changed. The city’s heartbeat carried on—morning tea brewing in kitchens, markets buzzing with familiar faces, buses rumbling down crowded streets. But underneath all that, there was this quiet tension, like everyone was waiting for the other shoe to drop.
News from Europe kept getting worse. You could almost feel the uncertainty woven into every conversation. Most folks tried to stick to their routines—maybe hoping that if they just kept doing what they always did, nothing would actually change.
Picture a woman in her middle years. Her days are filled with the little comforts: keeping her house in order, preparing meals, writing letters to loved ones. Yet, no matter how hard she tries to focus on the ordinary, her mind keeps drifting back to thoughts of air raids and whether her family will be safe. The radio’s always on in the background—sometimes, its updates are reassuring, other times, they just add to the worry. But she can’t turn it off; it’s her link to the world beyond her front door.
And it wasn’t just her. Neighbors would gather in kitchens or out on the stoop, swapping rumors, sharing what little they knew. Some were sure the danger would never actually reach them, brushing off the warnings. Others quietly started to prepare—buying extra tins of food, hanging blackout curtains just in case. Even the kids noticed something was up. They kept playing in the streets, their laughter echoing through the neighborhoods, but you could tell they sensed the grown-ups’ unease.
Then, the mood of the whole city shifted. When war was finally declared, it didn’t come with chaos or noise, but with a deep, heavy silence. People stopped what they were doing, gathered around radios, and listened as the Prime Minister’s voice confirmed what so many had feared. There wasn’t panic—just this collective pause, as everyone tried to take in what the future might hold.
Over the next few weeks, life started to change in ways both big and small. Gas masks became as common as overcoats, always close at hand. Air raid shelters popped up in gardens and parks, reminders that life could be interrupted at any moment. Still, a lot of people hung onto the hope that maybe, just maybe, the worst wouldn’t happen.
That woman at the center of it all found herself thinking about how fragile peace really is. She noticed how quickly her neighbors adjusted, how routines didn’t vanish—they just bent a little. Shops kept opening, the post was still delivered, and families came together for Sunday dinners, holding on to normal life as best they could. But underneath, there was this new sense of determination—almost like a promise that, no matter what came next, they’d face it together.
It became clear that war wasn’t just something happening far away. It seeped into every part of daily life. Suddenly, the line between the ordinary and the extraordinary faded, and the whole city braced itself for what was to come.

Chapter 2: First Air Raids — Fear, Confusion, and the Search for Safety
Picture this: one quiet evening in London, the wailing of air raid sirens suddenly slices through the night. Just like that, the city’s calm is gone—shattered in an instant. You can almost feel the panic ripple through the streets as families grab their children and whatever they can carry, racing for the underground stations. Not everyone moves right away. Some folks freeze, caught between doubt and fear. Should they trust the warning, or wait it out? That uncertainty—it's almost as terrifying as the danger itself.
In one home, a family squeezes together in the hallway, hoping it’s the safest spot. The mother tries her best to sound calm for her kids, but her hands won’t stop shaking. Outside, the distant thud of bombs serves as a grim reminder: the war is right here, right now. With the blackout in place, even familiar streets seem strange, swallowed up by darkness.
Those first few nights? They’re the toughest. Sleep comes in short bursts, always interrupted by sirens or the steady drone of planes overhead. People start to pick up on the subtle differences in each sound—learning which siren means danger, and which means relief. Some folks cling to routine, making tea, reading by candlelight, or telling stories just to pass the time. But for others, the fear is relentless, their nerves stretched thin with every passing hour.
As these raids keep coming, the city slowly adapts. You’d see air raid wardens walking the dim streets, making sure everyone’s safe and no light sneaks through the blackout curtains. Neighbors start looking out for one another, trading news and offering comfort wherever they can. Down in the shelters, strangers become fast friends—bonded by the simple fact that they’re all in this together.
One evening, imagine a woman sitting in a packed shelter, surrounded by people from every corner of the city. The air is thick with worry, but there’s also this unexpected sense of togetherness. Someone pulls out a deck of cards, and before long, laughter fills the space—even as everyone keeps one wary eye on the ceiling, as if a good joke might somehow hold back the bombs.
Here’s something to remember: fear never really goes away, but it doesn’t have to take over. People find ways to cope—through humor, habits, and simply being together. London’s resilience doesn’t come from grand gestures, but from small, everyday acts of courage, repeated over and over, night after night.
Searching for safety becomes the new normal. Every raid leaves a scar, sure—but it also uncovers a hidden strength in the city’s heart. London holds on, not because it’s fearless, but because it refuses to be broken.

Chapter 3: Everyday Life Under Siege—Adapting to the New Normal
Weeks drifted into months, and slowly, the rhythms of wartime life took hold. That first jolt of fear from the air raids? It faded to a kind of gritty acceptance. People learned to live with the constant threat, weaving danger into their daily routines. What used to feel extraordinary soon became just another part of life—and survival meant knowing how to adapt.
Picture this: in a quiet neighborhood, a mother gets up before dawn. Her motions are quick, almost automatic—she checks the windows for damage, sweeps away broken glass, and makes sure the blackout curtains are tight. Her kids rush through getting dressed, slipping gas masks next to their books and pencils into their schoolbags. The walk to school is hushed now, the streets lined with rubble, each step a reminder of what’s changed.
Shops would swing open as soon as the all-clear sounded, even if their shelves looked a little bare. Rationing forced everyone to get creative—stretching ingredients, inventing new recipes, and sharing tips with neighbors. Sure, people missed certain foods, and those shortages became the talk of the day. But most just shrugged it off, because deep down, everyone knew they were in this together.
Work life didn’t just stop. It shifted, sometimes interrupted by the blare of sirens or the call to serve. Some people became air raid wardens, others drove ambulances or helped at first aid posts. Suddenly, the line between private and public life blurred, and helping the community mattered more than ever. Evenings were spent in bomb shelters or at home, huddled around the radio, waiting for any scrap of news.
But here’s something beautiful: even with all the hardship, there were still sparks of joy. Maybe a neighbor shared a rare tin of peaches, or kids found a way to play among the ruins. Birthdays were marked with whatever treats could be found, and sometimes laughter would fill the air in places you’d never expect. Finding light in the darkness became a real-life superpower.
There was one afternoon, for example, when a woman paused from her chores and watched a group of children skipping rope right there in the street. Their laughter rose above the distant wail of sirens—a small but powerful sign that life kept moving, even when the world felt upside down. She felt a quiet gratitude for these little moments, knowing they mattered just as much as any act of heroism.
What did all this reveal? That resilience isn’t just a single, grand gesture. It’s a series of choices—made every single day. People adapted, not because they had to, but because they wouldn’t let fear run the show. The spirit of the city lived on, shaped by countless acts of everyday courage. That’s what truly defined each day under siege.

Chapter Four: Family, Friendship, and the Weight of Uncertainty.
Let’s talk about a time when families and friends faced challenges they’d never imagined. Wartime changed everything. Suddenly, separation became normal—loved ones packed their bags for the armed forces, or were sent off to safer places.
It’s hard to picture, isn’t it? Waiting for a letter, not knowing if it’ll bring good news or heartbreak. Each note that arrived in the mailbox was more than just words—it was hope, a lifeline tying people together across the miles.
Imagine a mother, standing in her kitchen, watching her sons get ready to leave for military service. She hides her worry behind gentle reminders—maybe a warm scarf, or a last-minute bit of advice. After they’re gone, the house feels so much quieter, every chore echoing with memories. She keeps busy with volunteering, but her heart is never far from her boys, wondering what dangers they’re facing.
And then, there are friendships. When life gets tough, you really find out who you can count on. Neighbors who used to just nod in passing now lean on each other—sharing stories, food, and even a little laughter in bomb shelters. Suddenly, strangers become part of your support system, and everyone starts looking out for one another.
Kids weren’t spared from all this, either. Some were sent away to the countryside—safe from bombs, but not from homesickness. They missed their families, struggled to fit in, and grew up faster than they should have. Meanwhile, the kids who stayed behind learned how to make sense of a world turned upside down. Their innocence gave way to resilience, shaped by the realities of war.
Picture this: a group of women gathered around a kitchen table. Some are laughing, some are on the verge of tears. They talk about husbands and sons who are far from home, the hassle of rationing, and the tiny victories that make the days a little easier. Just being together, sharing those worries, makes the load feel lighter—even if only for a moment.
What really stands out is that the emotional toll of war was just as real as any physical threat. Uncertainty wore people down day after day, but it also pulled them closer. Family and friendship became more than just words—they were lifelines, keeping everyone afloat when things seemed darkest.
The city’s strength? It didn’t come from any one person’s courage—it came from the connections between people. In the middle of so much loss and worry, those relationships offered comfort, hope, and the courage to keep moving forward.

Chapter 5: Reflections on Society, Politics, and the Meaning of Endurance
As the war dragged on, you can imagine how everyone started reflecting on the bigger forces shaping their lives. Day after day, survival was a challenge—and all of it played out against the backdrop of politics and national events.
News from the front lines trickled into every home. Sometimes, that news sparked heated debates. Other times, it fueled both hope and frustration.
Picture one family, gathered around the radio. The broadcasts are always on, dissected and discussed over every meal. They’re tracking the war’s shifting fortunes with a mix of anxiety and determination. Some folks start to question the choices their leaders are making, while others put their faith in the government, hoping it’ll get them through. There’s this powerful sense of being part of something bigger than yourself—it’s comforting, but honestly, it can be pretty overwhelming too.
Society itself seemed to transform under the weight of war. Old divisions, the kind that used to keep people apart, began to fade. In the shelters, class just didn’t matter—everyone faced the same dangers. Women, especially, stepped into new roles. They managed households, volunteered, and supported the war effort in ways that, before, often went unnoticed. Suddenly, their contributions weren’t just important—they were essential for the city’s survival.
But living through war brought up some big questions about what it really means to endure. What does it look like to keep going, even when every day brings new threats? How do you find purpose in the middle of so much chaos? For a lot of people, the answer was in those small acts of kindness and solidarity that shaped each day.
Take one afternoon: a woman stops what she’s doing to help her neighbor clear debris from a bombed-out house. The work is hard—no doubt about it—but there’s this real sense of accomplishment. In that moment, it’s not about who’s who or where you’re from; it’s about a shared commitment to rebuilding, side by side.
Endurance, it turns out, isn’t just about surviving. It’s about finding meaning in the struggle. The war pushed people to examine their values, to confront their own limits, and to discover unexpected strengths.
Through it all, the spirit of the city endured—thanks to countless acts of resilience and compassion that played out in big and small ways, every single day.
The story of London during the Blitz isn’t just about destruction. It’s a story of adaptation, solidarity, and hope. When faced with the unimaginable, ordinary people found extraordinary strength. And those experiences—the quiet moments, the daily routines of wartime life—give us a real window into what human endurance and renewal truly look like.

Chapter 6: The Rhythm of Danger—Nightly Raids and the Pulse of the City.
As autumn set in, have you ever noticed how the whole city seems to breathe in time with the dangers of the night? Each evening, as dusk crept across the skyline, you could actually feel the change—like an invisible signal passing through the air. Streets would quiet down, and folks moved with a purpose. Curtains got pulled tight, gas masks checked and re-checked. There was this shared, heavy anticipation. You could sense it—everyone knowing that, for the next few hours, life would play out under a cloud of uncertainty.
Picture a small flat, tucked somewhere above those silent streets. A father gathers his family in the sitting room, waiting and listening for that first wail of the siren. The kids, who once fidgeted and squabbled, now quietly pack their favorite books, maybe a battered old deck of cards, getting ready for another night in the shelter below. Their mother, looking tired but calm, checks the emergency supplies—just a flask of tea, a tin of biscuits, and a torch whose batteries are growing weak.
The raids themselves became, strangely enough, part of the routine. The distant hum of engines, the sharp whistle of bombs falling, the ground shuddering beneath you—these weren’t just sounds anymore; they marked the hours as surely as any clock. Some nights, the danger would pass fast, leaving only the echo of fear behind. But on others, the city shook for what felt like forever, and those shelters felt like both a safe haven and a prison.
In that darkness, people still managed to keep hope alive. Imagine a young man, who used to be a clerk, now spinning stories for the children—tales of distant lands and brave heroes. There’s an elderly woman, knitting by candlelight, her hands trembling but steady enough to offer comfort with every click of the needles. And every so often, laughter would bubble up—softer, yes, but that much sweeter. It was proof that even in the worst moments, you could still find little sparks of joy.
It became clear that the city’s strength wasn't just about surviving the danger. It was about finding a rhythm within it. Nightly raids were terrifying, no doubt, but they also pulled people together in ways peace never could. That shared experience—of fear, of hope, of simply making it through—created bonds that would outlast any raid.
Most of us don’t realize how quickly the extraordinary becomes, well, just ordinary. The nightly rituals, the whispered reassurances, the quiet acts of kindness—these little things became the threads that held the city close. In the face of constant danger, Londoners learned not just to endure fear, but to live right alongside it.

Chapter 7: Loss, Grief, and the Quiet Work of Carrying On
With every new week, the true cost of war felt more and more personal. Streets you once strolled, maybe even whistling, were now scarred with craters and mounds of broken brick. And when news of casualties reached the city, it landed with a heavy, irreversible finality. Suddenly, the absence of someone—a neighbor, a friend—showed up in the smallest ways. There’s a missing voice at the market, an empty chair at the dinner table. Picture this: one morning, a shopkeeper is sweeping broken glass from his doorway. Every movement is slow, careful. Just the night before, a bomb dropped nearby—windows shattered, his goods scattered across the sidewalk. He stops for a moment, glancing at a family photo tucked behind the counter. That wave of loss presses down on him. But there are still customers to help, and so he opens the door with a tired, determined smile. Grief became a constant companion, but it didn’t storm in loud and obvious. Instead, it crept in quietly—maybe over a cup of tea, or while folding laundry in the soft, flickering light of a shelter. People learned to carry their sorrow, to tuck it away just enough so life could go on. Funerals happened, sometimes rushed and always hushed, and letters of condolence were written with trembling hands, each word chosen with care. Still, even surrounded by loss, there was this stubborn will to keep going. Imagine a teacher, her classroom now just a handful of students, leading lessons in a borrowed church hall. The kids, faces pale but determined, clung to the comfort of spelling and arithmetic. Those familiar routines gave everyone a little piece of stability—a gentle reminder that the world hadn’t completely fallen apart. Over time, it became clear: grief didn’t weaken the city. If anything, it deepened its resolve. The quiet, everyday work of carrying on—of rebuilding, of remembering—turned into its own quiet act of defiance. Most folks realized, when faced with loss, the only way forward was together. The real endurance of the city wasn’t measured by how many buildings still stood. No, it was seen in the way people managed to hold onto hope, even as they mourned everything—and everyone—they’d lost.

Chapter Eight: Small Joys and the Persistence of Hope.
Even in the midst of rationing and rubble, hope had a way of sneaking in, almost when you least expected it.
Think about the little things—a warm loaf of bread, a letter from someone you missed, or just a patch of blue sky after a long, rainy night. Suddenly, these became treasures. People started to really savor these moments, letting even the smallest joys fill the empty spaces left behind by fear and loss.
One afternoon, a handful of neighbors decided to gather in what used to be a garden, now bombed-out and battered. They didn’t have much—hard soil, barely any tools—but they were determined to plant a few rows of vegetables. Just the act of digging, of putting something new in the ground, felt like a promise to the future.
The children joined in, their hands caked in mud, faces lit up with laughter. That little garden—humble as it was—became a symbol of resilience. It showed everyone that life could find a way, even in the harshest conditions.
Celebrations didn’t stop either. Birthdays rolled around, sometimes with makeshift cakes and songs sung quietly in shelters. Couples still found ways to share a tender glance, a little joke, even as the world outside seemed to fall apart. And if you listened closely, you’d still hear the shouts of kids playing in parks, even those marked by bomb craters.
What really stood out was realizing that hope isn’t always this huge, dramatic thing. Most of the time, it's found in the little choices—sharing what you have at dinner, tending a tiny garden, or just pausing to watch the sunrise. These moments didn’t erase the pain, but they balanced it out, giving people a reason to keep moving forward.
In the end, the city’s real strength was its persistence of hope. Even when everything seemed stacked against them, Londoners chose to believe that better days might come. Their optimism wasn’t loud or showy—it was quiet, steady, and it shaped the way they lived, day after day.

Chapter 9: The Changing Face of Community—New Roles and Responsibilities
As the war dragged on, the entire feel of community life started to shift. The old routines? They were changing. People who used to lean on others suddenly found themselves stepping up, taking the lead. And folks who’d been in the background for years? They were discovering just how strong they could be.
Picture this: a young woman, who’d always been shy and unsure, ends up becoming the go-to organizer for her street’s air raid shelter. She keeps track of the supplies, makes sure shifts are covered, and always has a moment to listen when someone needs to talk. Week by week, her confidence grows, and before long, her neighbors are counting on her steady, reassuring presence.
Then, across town, there’s a retired railway worker. He decides he’s going to check on the elderly and anyone stuck at home, bringing them groceries and sharing the latest news from outside. His regular visits become a lifeline, and people start to look forward to the quiet kindness he brings. The gratitude and respect he earns—well, it’s hard to put into words.
Even the kids get involved. Some pitch in with chores, or dash out on errands for neighbors. Others come up with games and little performances to keep everyone’s spirits up in the shelters. Their energy and imagination aren’t just entertaining—they’re a real comfort, a reminder that the future is still wide open.
What really stands out here is how community isn’t just about where you live. It’s about what you share—your purpose, your effort. As everyone picked up these new responsibilities, that old line between “us” and “them” began to fade. People started to feel like they truly belonged, because they were working together for something bigger.
That’s where the city’s strength came from—its ability to adapt, and to see the unique talents and needs of every person. In the tough times of war, Londoners learned something powerful: everyone can contribute, and when you face challenges together, survival becomes a shared achievement.

Let’s talk about Chapter Ten: “The Long Haul: Fatigue, Doubt, and the Struggle to Endure.”
By the time the second winter of the Blitz rolled in, exhaustion had settled over London like a thick, endless fog.
That first burst of adrenaline? It was gone. And what replaced it was a bone-deep weariness that just wouldn’t let go. Nights in the shelters seemed to stretch on forever, and the chill wasn’t just in the air—it found its way right into people’s bones and hearts.
Remember all those early promises of a quick victory? Well, reality set in. This was going to be a long, hard road.
Picture a family huddled together in their home. A mother, running on empty, finds herself snapping at her kids more than she’d like. She’s quick to apologize, but you can still see the worry etched into her face. Her husband, once so full of hope, now talks less about what’s next and more about just making it through another day.
And then, doubt starts to creep in. People begin to wonder—are all these sacrifices really worth it? Can the city actually survive another year of bombing and shortages? The news is confusing, sometimes even scary. And when information is scarce, rumors—about defeat, or even betrayal—spread like wildfire.
But even when fatigue felt overwhelming, there were these little sparks of hope. Maybe a neighbor would offer a warm smile or a few kind words. Or perhaps a stranger would share a bit of their precious, rationed food. It’s these small acts, these reminders that no one is truly alone, that really kept people going.
Endurance, it turns out, isn’t some steady, unbroken line. It’s more like a series of hills and valleys. Strength comes and goes. And it’s perfectly normal to feel tired, discouraged—even hopeless—sometimes. The real trick is to just keep moving forward. Find rest when you can, and don’t be afraid to lean on others.
The city’s resilience wasn’t about never being scared, or never having doubts. It was about persistence—even when things seemed impossible. Londoners slowly realized you could be scared and brave at the same time. And that surviving wasn’t just about grit and courage, but also about taking care of yourself and those around you.

Chapter 11: The War’s Turning Point—Signs of Change and the Return of Hope
As the months slipped by, things started to shift—though at first, it was almost too subtle to notice. The raids that once felt endless grew less frequent, and the city, with all its scars, slowly began to heal.
You could feel it in the air. Suddenly, there were fewer sirens wailing through the night. Birds returned to their morning songs, and those heavy, anxious silences gave way to the sounds of life coming back—shops opening their doors, schools welcoming students again.
One morning, a group of children walked to school—this time, without the familiar burden of gas masks slung over their shoulders. Their laughter rang out brighter, their steps felt lighter. Teachers greeted them at the gates with cautious smiles, not quite letting their guard down, but daring to hope that maybe, just maybe, the worst had passed.
And it wasn’t just the children. Adults began to let themselves hope too. Imagine a father, usually quiet and reserved, suddenly talking about the future—a new business idea, maybe a holiday by the sea, or even planting a garden when spring arrived. Parks that had been deserted filled up again, as folks tried to reclaim a sense of normal life, reconnecting with friends and neighbors under the open sky.
Here’s something that really stands out: hope wasn’t just a feeling anymore—it was something people practiced. By searching for the smallest signs of improvement, they could start to picture a life beyond the war. Even the simplest pleasures—a warm cup of tea in a sunny kitchen, a stroll down familiar streets—became little milestones on their journey back to normal.
The city’s spirit, battered but never broken, began to shine through again. Londoners discovered that healing was possible, even after their darkest nights. And maybe most importantly, they realized the future wasn’t just something to survive—it was something they could create, together.

Chapter 12: Looking Back—Memory, Meaning, and the Legacy of the Blitz
As the war drew to a close, people in London couldn’t help but look back on everything that had changed. The city, even with its scars, stood tall—a true symbol of endurance. Memories of fear and loss mingled with moments of courage, kindness, and hope.
Picture this: a woman sits quietly by her window, watching the sun dip behind the rooftops. She’s thinking about friends she’s lost, neighbors who became like family, and all those tiny acts of bravery that helped her get through. The city she sees now feels older, wiser—and deeply marked by everything it’s survived.
The children who grew up during those years carried the war’s lessons with them. They remembered huddling in shelters at night, playing games by candlelight, and swapping stories to pass the time. Sure, their innocence was shaped by what they’d lived through, but their ability to find joy? That never faded.
Over time, it became clear—the true legacy of the Blitz wasn’t just in the buildings that were rebuilt, or the lives that were lost. It was in the way people came together. Most folks realized that, at the end of the day, it was all about the bonds they’d formed, the hope they held onto, and all those quiet moments of resilience that truly defined the experience.
The story of wartime London wasn’t about perfect heroism. It was about everyday people facing challenges they never expected. Their memories—captured in diaries or shared over a simple cup of tea—became a kind of blueprint for endurance. They remind us that, even in the darkest times, the human spirit can find a way... to keep going, to heal, and to hope again.

As we wrap up our journey through the story of London during the Blitz, it’s clear this isn’t just about bombs falling or city streets plunged into darkness. It’s a true story of ordinary people discovering a quiet strength, right in the heart of chaos. Through the pages of that wartime diary, we see a city not simply surviving, but being transformed—by kindness, by resilience, and by the quiet power of hope.
So, what can you take from their experience, especially when life throws its own curveballs your way?
The first thing: small acts of kindness really can hold a community together, even when the world feels upside down. Resilience isn’t about big, heroic gestures—it’s built, day by day, in the little choices you make. Hope? It’s something you practice. You find it in shared smiles, in laughter, in those tiny moments that remind you you’re not alone.
Endurance means you don’t have to be fearless. You just need to keep moving, even when doubt and fear are right there with you. And true community? That’s shaped in tough times, not just when everything’s easy.
Here’s what this means for you: the lessons from the Blitz aren’t locked away in history. They’re alive every time you reach out, adapt, or choose to hope. When things feel uncertain, look for those small joys—a neighbor’s wave, a shared meal, a quiet laugh. Let those moments be your shelter.
Remember, you don’t have to be unbreakable to get through hard times. Like those Londoners, you can find strength in your connections, meaning even when things are tough, and hope in the promise of a new day. The story of the Blitz reminds us: even when the night is at its darkest, dawn will come—and with it, a chance to begin again.
